interactions.label: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, firm, non-transilluminant swelling i

params.question: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, firm, non-transilluminant swelling in his right testis noticed two weeks ago. What should be the primary clinical concern?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epididymitis is typically painful and tender, not painless. A painless firm testicular mass in a young man raises a far more serious concern.
Torsion presents with acute severe pain and a high-riding testis, not a painless mass noticed over weeks.

Correct. In men aged 15–35, a painless solid testicular mass is cancer until proven otherwise. Germ cell tumours are the most common solid malignancy in this age group, and over 95% of Stage I cases are cured with cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
A hydrocele transilluminates and feels fluctuant. This mass is firm and non-transilluminant, pointing to a solid lesion — malignancy must be excluded first.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key rule: a painless, firm testicular mass in a man aged 15–35 is a germ cell tumour until proven otherwise. Delay worsens staging and prognosis.
Exactly right. Early recognition of a painless testicular mass as a probable germ cell tumour is the single most important factor in achieving cure.

params.question: A testicular tumour shows a homogeneous, creamy-white cut surface with no haemorrhage. Microscopy reveals uniform large round cells with clear cytoplasm, prominent central nucleoli, and dense lymphocytic infiltrate within fibrous septa. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Embryonal carcinoma has a haemorrhagic, variegated cut surface with highly pleomorphic cells forming solid sheets and gland-like spaces — the gross appearance alone rules it out here.

Correct. The homogeneous creamy-white surface, large round cells with clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm, prominent central nucleoli, and pathognomonic lymphocytic septa all define seminoma. Normal alpha-fetoprotein confirms it has not been reclassified.
Yolk sac tumour is defined by Schiller-Duval bodies and characteristically raises serum alpha-fetoprotein. Neither finding is present here.
Choriocarcinoma characteristically has a microscopic, haemorrhagic primary with massive distant metastases. Diagnosis requires both cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts together.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the gross rule: homogeneous, creamy-white = seminoma. Variegated and haemorrhagic = non-seminomatous GCT. Then confirm with microscopy and markers.
Well done. The gross rule is your first-pass tool: homogeneous and cream-white means seminoma; variegated with haemorrhage points to a non-seminomatous tumour.

params.question: Benign prostatic hyperplasia predisposes to prostatic adenocarcinoma because both diseases arise from the same anatomical zone of the prostate.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. BPH originates in the transition zone flanking the proximal urethra, while adenocarcinoma arises separately in the peripheral zone. They have unrelated pathogenesis, so BPH does not predispose to cancer despite frequently coexisting in the same patient.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. BPH arises in the transition zone and adenocarcinoma in the peripheral zone — anatomically distinct regions with unrelated molecular mechanisms. Their frequent coexistence in elderly men is coincidental, not causal.

interactions.label: A 72-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostatic adenocarcinoma develops severe lo

params.question: A 72-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostatic adenocarcinoma develops severe low back pain. Imaging reveals multiple dense, sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis. Which statement best explains this finding?

answers.text: Prostatic carcinoma produces osteolytic bone metastases similar to most other carcinomas

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Most carcinomas produce osteolytic (bone-destroying) metastases, but prostatic adenocarcinoma is a notable exception. Its bone deposits are characteristically osteoblastic — dense and sclerotic.

answers.text: Direct tumour invasion from the seminal vesicles into adjacent vertebrae causes sclerosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Seminal vesicle invasion indicates T3b staging but is a local event. Distant sclerotic spinal and pelvic lesions result from haematogenous spread, not direct extension.

answers.text: Haematogenous spread produces characteristically osteoblastic bone metastases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Prostatic adenocarcinoma bone metastases are characteristically osteoblastic, producing dense sclerotic lesions. Alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated. On bone scintigraphy, a superscan may be seen where skeletal uptake is so intense that the kidneys become invisible.

answers.text: Lymphatic spread via pelvic nodes deposits tumour cells in the vertebral periosteum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pelvic lymph nodes are involved in prostatic carcinoma spread, but the dense sclerotic bone deposits result from haematogenous metastasis, not lymphatic drainage.

overallFeedback.feedback: Prostatic adenocarcinoma produces characteristically osteoblastic (bone-forming) metastases, unlike the osteolytic deposits of most other carcinomas. Elevated alkaline phosphatase and a bone scintigraphy superscan are associated findings.
Well done. Osteoblastic bone metastases are a hallmark of prostatic adenocarcinoma — a key distinguishing feature from the osteolytic deposits of most other carcinomas.

params.question: A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a bright red, velvety patch on the glans penis. Biopsy shows full-thickness squamous dysplasia with an intact basement membrane. Which diagnosis is most likely?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Condyloma acuminatum is caused by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 and shows koilocytosis without dysplasia. It presents as a cauliflower-like wart, not a red velvety patch.

Bowen disease presents as a thickened greyish plaque on the keratinised penile shaft skin. The glans is mucosal and lacks surface keratin, so a red velvety lesion there points to a different diagnosis.
Invasive squamous cell carcinoma breaches the basement membrane by definition. This biopsy shows full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane — it remains a premalignant lesion.

Correct. A bright red velvety patch on the mucosal glans with full-thickness dysplasia and an intact basement membrane defines erythroplasia of Queyrat. The glans lacks surface keratin, which accounts for the red moist appearance — distinguishing it from Bowen disease on the keratinised shaft.

overallFeedback.feedback: Among penile intraepithelial neoplasia lesions, location distinguishes them: erythroplasia of Queyrat is a red velvety patch on the mucosal glans, while Bowen disease is a greyish plaque on the keratinised shaft. Both show full-thickness dysplasia with an intact basement membrane.
Exactly. Location is the key distinguishing feature among penile intraepithelial neoplasia lesions: glans (mucosal) = erythroplasia of Queyrat; shaft (keratinised skin) = Bowen disease.
